html:
The Pilbara is a large, dry region of red ranges and plains in the north of Western Australia, between the Indian Ocean coast and the Great Sandy Desert. Its rocks are among the oldest on Earth, and it holds some of the world's richest iron ore.

It has been home to Aboriginal peoples for tens of thousands of years, among them the Yindjibarndi and Ngarluma of the Fortescue and Roebourne country, the Banjima of the Hamersley Range, the Nyamal and Palyku in the east and the Kariyarra on the coast.

British settlers brought sheep from the 1860s. In 1946 Aboriginal station workers walked off the stations in the Pilbara strike, which lasted about three years.

From the 1960s huge open pit iron mines made it a main supplier of ore to Japan and later China. In 2020 a mining company blew up the ancient rock shelters of Juukan Gorge, sacred to the Puutu Kunti Kurrama and Pinikura peoples, causing a public outcry.
